comparator.name: Security Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The current catalogue and regulations confirm 180 EC, with 60 EC in each year and no specialisation. Years one and two are compulsory. In year three, students take 30 EC of electives before a 15 EC thesis, 10 EC Integrated Project 2 and 5 EC Governance of Security. Integrated Project 1 must be passed before Integrated Project 2. Thesis entry requires all year-one credits, 45 year-two credits and a complete research methods sequence.
components: Compulsory group project on a challenge related to gender-based violence.
Individual research thesis. Requires all first-year credits, at least 45 second-year credits and the prescribed research methods sequence.
Team policy advice for a security or safety practitioner. Students must first pass Integrated Project 1.
Students choose approved electives, a minor, an internship, study abroad or a combination.

routeSelection.basis: The 2026–27 OER states that Security Studies has no specialisations. The reconstruction therefore follows the full target-named compulsory curriculum and preserves the programme’s 30-EC elective space without selecting a minor, internship or exchange destination to improve UCR fit.

core: Interdisciplinary analysis of contemporary safety and security challenges
Threats, actors, vital interests and multi-level security governance
Crisis prevention, preparedness, disaster response and public-health resilience
Law, public institutions and public–private security cooperation
Scientific security research, data analysis and policy advice
Economics, welfare and the protection of vital societal interests
adjacent: Psychological, historical and societal dimensions of threat and extremism
questions: How should governments and institutions analyse and respond to complex security threats?
How can societies prepare for crises and coordinate response and recovery?
How should law, institutions and technical systems govern cyber threats?

alternatives.label: Security, Conflict and Governance
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum combines security institutions, conflict and peace, law, history, economics, extremism, data and mixed research methods; the label describes that broad centre of gravity.
alternatives.concept: Study political institutions, conflict, public law and the history of warfare. Explore responses to violent extremism and use qualitative methods, data analysis and economics to investigate questions about conflict and governance.
progression: Law and statistics foundations precede criminal, international and EU law and applied econometrics. Historical, political and empirical work develops across the six terms.

alternatives.label: Disaster Risk and Societal Resilience
alternatives.labelReason: Natural hazards, public health, climate risk, social behaviour, law, governance, data and applied partner research form a coherent crisis-preparedness and recovery route.
alternatives.concept: Study how natural hazards, climate change and disease outbreaks affect communities. Use psychology, sociology and public policy to examine vulnerability and collective responses. Begin with a team inquiry into a regional sustainability problem, then develop skills in behavioural statistics and qualitative research.
progression: The team sustainability project introduces applied inquiry in the first term alongside public-health and governance foundations. Hazard science and social psychology support later work on vulnerability and governance, with statistical and qualitative methods developed across the plan.
alternatives.distinctness: Adds public health, hazard science, climate change, social and behavioural science, sustainability governance and a regional team project.

alternatives.label: Digital Systems and Security Governance
alternatives.labelReason: Programming, networks, operating systems, databases, algorithms and AI are combined with law and international and European governance.
alternatives.concept: Study how networks, operating systems and databases work. Combine programming, data analysis and AI ethics with international relations, public law and European governance to examine the policy questions raised by digital systems.
progression: Programming precedes networks, algorithms and AI decision methods. Mathematical Methods precedes deep learning, the law gateway precedes the advanced law courses, and Research Methods & Statistics precedes Econometrics.
alternatives.distinctness: Adds computing systems, programming and mathematical foundations, algorithms and AI ethics. The overlap in law, conflict and institutions supplies context for digital governance.

selection.assessment: Three distinct feasible programmes cover security and conflict broadly, disaster risk and resilience, or digital systems and security governance. The digital direction is grounded in the current optional minor and supported by the required Cyber Threats module.

blocks: Security, political institutions, conflict and history
Both examine the causes of conflict and approaches to peacebuilding through multiple disciplines.
Both consider violent extremism and responses to it. UCR focuses on protective factors and prevention among young people.
Leiden introduces security and safety as a field across several disciplines.
Leiden uses Syria as a sustained case study in conflict and security.
Leiden examines how societies identify and protect vital assets, interests and values.
Law, crime and economics of security
Both examine international law in relation to state responses and the use of force. Leiden also considers legal responses to terrorism, cyberattacks and cross-border crime.
Leiden applies economic reasoning directly to safety and security, including issues such as sanctions.
Crisis, disaster, health and societal resilience
Both investigate disaster risks and responses. Leiden centres on the Fukushima accident, while UCR studies how geoscience can inform risk reduction across hazards.
Both teach statistical analysis for empirical questions. UCR emphasises experimental design and behavioural data, while Leiden includes survey research.
Both involve team inquiry into a problem supplied by an external organisation. Leiden develops security policy advice, while UCR investigates a regional sustainability question.
Both examine how institutions and networks govern collective problems. UCR applies this lens to sustainability.
Both cover technical foundations of networked systems. Leiden also examines threats and responses from policy and societal perspectives.
Skills, research methods, projects and open space
Both develop academic work and communication skills. Leiden teaches and assesses those skills within Security Studies.
Both introduce research design and the use of evidence. UCR includes descriptive and inferential statistics.
Both develop qualitative research design, interviewing and interpretation. Leiden applies these methods within Security Studies.
Leiden develops research, data interpretation and debating skills in its second lab.
Leiden integrates safety analysis, teamwork and communication in its third lab.
Leiden requires a team project on gender-based violence.
Leiden requires a 15 EC individual Security Studies thesis.
Leiden reserves 30 EC for student-selected study.

notes.text: Leiden requires a sequence of Security Studies labs, case studies, two integrated projects and an individual thesis. The UCR options bring together related courses and methods from several disciplines. The digital systems option draws on the themes of an elective Leiden minor and the required Cyber Threats course.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Security Studies degree examines how societies understand and respond to threats. Students study conflict, disasters, law and cyber threats through case studies and research methods, then develop policy advice and write a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options focus on security and conflict, disaster risk and resilience, or digital systems and governance. Leiden teaches these areas through a dedicated security curriculum, with skills labs and projects that connect them across the degree.

curriculum.limitation: The degree includes 150 EC of required study and 30 EC of electives. The second integrated project requires passing the first. The thesis requires completing year one, earning at least 45 EC in year two and passing the required research methods courses.
